_comment: Signora's signal catalog — the global vocabulary of commercial hypotheses. Belongs to Signora, not to any customer: a workspace configures which of these matter to it and how centrally, and can never invent a type. That constraint is what makes AI reasoning, benchmarking, analytics, documentation, and support able to speak about signals across customers at all. Every hypothesis is phrased as a possibility, never a fact — a signal proposes a commercial reading, it does not assert one. Reviewed like code; a change here is a release. `limitations` and `suggested_validation` were added 2026-07-30 (M9, T126) and are owned here rather than by the AI Reasoning Engine: what a signal type does NOT imply is a property of the type, identical across every account and every day, so generating it per reasoning call would pay for it every time and get a subtly different answer every time (ADR-0030, Decision 5). They are ENGINEERING-AUTHORED PENDING DOMAIN REVIEW — written to be honest rather than authoritative, and a domain expert should revise them; that is exactly why they live in a reviewed, versioned artifact instead of a prompt.

types.title: Expansion opportunity
types.hypothesis: Sustained investment across several fronts suggests the company is adding capacity, and may be open to tools that support growth.
types.why_it_matters: Companies investing ahead of growth buy differently from companies holding steady — they are budgeting for capability they do not yet have.
limitations: Investment ahead of growth says nothing about budget for *your* category — capacity spend is often funded by cutting elsewhere.
It does not indicate that a purchase decision is underway, only that the company is adding capability.
Growth in one division does not imply growth in the one you sell to.
suggested_validation: Check which functions the recent hiring is in, and whether they are the ones that would use your product.
Ask on a first call which division the investment sits in — the signal cannot tell you.

types.title: Budget unlocked
types.hypothesis: New capital may free spending that was previously deferred.
types.why_it_matters: Funding changes what a company can approve, and often how quickly.
limitations: A funding round is not earmarked for any particular category. Most of it usually funds headcount and runway.
The round may have closed months before it was announced, so the money may already be committed.
It says nothing about who controls the spend.
suggested_validation: Read the round announcement for a stated use of funds.
Confirm the *close* date rather than the announcement date before treating this as recent.

types.title: Displacement opportunity
types.hypothesis: A retired system suggests a replacement decision that is recent, or imminent.
types.why_it_matters: The window in which a replacement is chosen is short, and it closes quietly.
limitations: A retired system may already have been replaced — retirement is often announced after the decision.
Retirement can mean consolidation onto an incumbent you also compete with, not an opening.
It does not identify who owns the replacement decision.
suggested_validation: Check the careers page for roles naming the replacement stack.
Search for a competitor's public announcement of the win before assuming the decision is open.

types.title: Modernization underway
types.hypothesis: Adopting and retiring systems together suggests a stack is being replaced rather than extended.
types.why_it_matters: A company mid-migration is already spending on change, and already comparing options.
limitations: Adoption and retirement happening together does not mean they concern the same system.
You may be seeing the end of a migration that was decided long ago, not the beginning of one.
It does not indicate the programme's scope or budget.
suggested_validation: Check whether the adopted and retired technologies serve the same function.
Look for an announced migration timeline; a published end date means the decision is behind you.

types.title: New decision maker
types.hypothesis: A newly appointed leader may re-examine what they inherited.
types.why_it_matters: New leaders are unusually willing to change arrangements they did not choose.
limitations: A new appointment carries no mandate to change vendors, and internal promotions usually continue existing commitments.
The appointee may not control the relevant budget.
It says nothing about dissatisfaction with an incumbent.
suggested_validation: Check whether the appointment was internal or external — an outside hire changes more than a promotion.
Look at the stack they ran at their previous employer.

types.title: Decision maker departed
types.hypothesis: A departure may stall decisions that leader was driving, or reopen ones already made.
types.why_it_matters: Both directions matter: an opportunity can be lost, and a closed decision can reopen.
limitations: A departure does not lapse existing contracts, and a successor may already be in place.
It may be a planned retirement rather than a disruption.
The vacancy may be filled internally by someone who owned the original decision.
suggested_validation: Check for an announced successor before treating the seat as open.
Check whether the departure was announced in advance, which usually means continuity was planned.

types.title: Active evaluation
types.hypothesis: Sustained research on a topic suggests an evaluation may already be under way.
types.why_it_matters: Arriving during an evaluation is a different conversation from starting one.
limitations: Intent data reflects what individuals researched, not an approved project.
The researcher may hold no budget and may not work in the buying function.
The topic may be adjacent to your category rather than in it.
suggested_validation: Confirm which function the research came from before treating it as a buying signal.
Look for a public RFP or tender, which is a decision rather than an interest.

types.title: Consolidation underway
types.hypothesis: An acquisition may force systems and budgets to be consolidated.
types.why_it_matters: Consolidation forces decisions that were being deferred, in both directions.
limitations: An announced acquisition is not a closed one, and tooling decisions usually wait quarters past close.
The acquirer's existing stack normally prevails, so this can close a door rather than open one.
It does not indicate which entity's contracts survive.
suggested_validation: Check whether the deal has actually closed.
Find out which side's systems are being retained — that decides whether this is an opening.

types.title: Contraction risk
types.hypothesis: A company reducing headcount or revenue may be re-scoping what it spends and who approves it.
types.why_it_matters: Contraction changes budget authority before it is announced — and it can mean either risk or an efficiency conversation.
limitations: Contraction does not mean spending stops; cost pressure often accelerates consolidation purchases.
It may reflect a divestiture rather than decline.
Company-wide figures can hide a division that is still growing.
suggested_validation: Check whether the decline is company-wide or confined to one division.
Look for a divestiture announcement that would explain the figures without indicating distress.
